panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (a, b). a: Sialendoscopic view of Stensen's duct showing debris partially obstructing the lumen, with the typical white ductal wall appearance described as diagnostic in juvenile recurrent parotitis. b: Sialendoscopic view of Stensen's duct showing ductal stenosis, with the typical white ductal wall appearance and scarce vascularity described as diagnostic sialendoscopic findings in juvenile recurrent parotitis.

in_text_mentions: of salivary diseases. It is a minimally invasive method using a semirigid optic endoscopic device. By inserting it through the oral cavity and papilla catheterization, it is possible to observe the anatomical course of Stensen's duct and any pathology involved with it. Sialoliths, sialectasia, and stenosis of the duct can be detected [15]. The most diagnostic sialendoscopic findings are the white ductal wall appearance and scarce vascularity in the ductal lumina along with confined/diffused stenosis and many fibrinous debris/mucous plugs that are seen very often in children (Figure 2) [1, 16].

panels.rationale: Single coronal MRI from a case report of juvenile recurrent parotitis in an 8-year-old boy. The caption and in-text mention specifically describe right acute-on-chronic parotiditis and chronic left parotiditis with atrophic changes, which is a direct manifestation of JRP. The image is a real patient radiology image and does not indicate third-party copyright.

panels.rationale: Single clinical photograph of an 8-year-old boy with right-sided parotid-region facial swelling, from a case report titled for juvenile recurrent parotitis; the visible swelling of the preauricular/cheek region is the disease's classic clinical manifestation, matching the vocabulary finding 'Swelling of the parotid region of the face'. The hypertrophic scar in front of the tragus is a post-surgical change (prior extraoral incision and drainage) and is recorded as a proposed finding rather than as the disease-defining manifestation. Skin (cheek, ear, neck) is adequately lit and appears light; age is stated in the caption; no ethnicity stated.

in_text_mentions: When firm pressure was applied over the gland, no purulent discharge was noticed from the parotid duct. However, a hypertrophic scar was noticed in front of the tragus on the right side from an extraoral incision and drainage for the same condition performed three months before the clinic visit in another hospital (Figure 1).

panels.rationale: Grayscale ultrasound of the left parotid gland in a case report titled 'The Parotid Puzzle: A Case of Juvenile Recurrent Parotitis.' The panel is a real patient image showing diffuse parotid parenchymal swelling with heterogeneous echogenicity and enlarged intraparotid lymph nodes, sonographic features the authors attribute to left parotitis in the context of juvenile recurrent parotitis (caption and in-text mentions explicitly support parotid swelling and intraparotid lymph nodes). Annotated with blue and green arrows. No patient demographics given in the caption, so age group is unknown; no skin visible, so skin tone is not applicable.
panels.attribution_text: M P et al. The Parotid Puzzle: A Case of Juvenile Recurrent Parotitis.. Cureus 2025. doi:10.7759/cureus.84786. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 2.
panels.figure_caption: Diffuse swelling of the left parotid gland parenchyma with increased echogenicity. Glandular parenchyma shows multiple different sizes intra parotid lymph nodes. No features of abscess formation. Blue arrow- Increased echogenicity of left parotid gland parenchyma; Green arrow- Intraparotid lymph node
in_text_mentions: Ultrasound during the first episode showed diffuse swelling of the parotid gland. The glandular parenchyma was heterogeneous and mixed with hyperechoic and hypoechoic areas. There were no features of abscess formation. There were no features of ductal dilatation or features of calcification or calculus formation. There were mildly enlarged intraparotid lymph nodes. The right parotid gland appeared normal. Usual lymph nodes were identified in the neck. Sonographic features were consistent with left parotitis (Figure 2).

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Ultrasound panel A from a case report of juvenile recurrent parotitis in a 4-year-old, showing multiple hypoechoic areas in the parotid parenchyma; this is the classic sonographic appearance of JRP. B: Ultrasound panel B from the same JRP case report shows color Doppler hypervascularization of the parotid gland parenchyma, supporting the diagnosis of JRP; the specific Doppler finding is not in the provided vocabulary, so it is proposed.

in_text_mentions: Diagnostic assessment: a panoramic radiography was performed to search for any dental infectious foci. In fact, no dental or alveolar bone anomalies were displayed (Figure 3). The USG images (Figure 4) showed the presence of multiple hypoechogenic areas and a hypervascularization within the parenchyma gland, confirming the diagnosis of JRP.

panels.rationale: Single-image ultrasound figure from a case report titled 'The Parotid Puzzle: A Case of Juvenile Recurrent Parotitis.' The panel shows the left parotid gland as mildly bulky and hypoechoic with multiple small hypoechoic intraparotid areas (blue arrows) and intraparotid lymph nodes (green arrow), matching the vocabulary finding of multiple small hypoechoic/cystic parotid lesions on ultrasound in juvenile recurrent parotitis. Modality, body site and findings are supported by the caption; no ethnicity or age is stated in the caption/in-text, and no skin is visible for tone assessment.
panels.attribution_text: M P et al. The Parotid Puzzle: A Case of Juvenile Recurrent Parotitis.. Cureus 2025. doi:10.7759/cureus.84786. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: Left parotid gland is mildly bulky and hypoechoic. Multiple small intraparotid lymphadenitis noted. Blue arrow- Hypoechoic areas; Green arrow- Intraparotid lymph nodes
in_text_mentions: echoic. Evidence of multiple intraparotid lymphadenitis was noted and measured at 1.2 cm. There was no evidence of necrosis/abscess formation. There was no evidence of parotid duct dilatation/calcification. The left submandibular gland was normal in size and echotexture. Evidence of multiple small left upper cervical lymphadenitis was noted, the largest one noted at the left submandibular region measuring 1.5 cm. There was no evidence of necrosis/abscess formation. The right side parotid gland was normal size and normal echotexture. No focal lesions were seen and no duct dilatation (Figure 1).

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Panel A shows left parotid region swelling, a classic clinical manifestation of juvenile recurrent parotitis, supported by the figure caption and the disease-focused article title. B: Panel B shows a left cervical lymph node in a case report of juvenile recurrent parotitis; the finding is nonspecific and not present in the vocabulary, but is captioned in the disease-focused case report, so attributed with lower confidence.
panels.attribution_text: Dammak et al. Juvenile recurrent parotitis in a 4-year-old patient: a case report.. The Pan African medical journal 2021. doi:10.11604/pamj.2021.40.86.27001. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: extraoral view: A) swelling of the left parotid region; B) presence of left cervical lymph node
in_text_mentions: Clinical findings: the extra oral examination (Figure 1) revealed a painful and firm swelling in the left parotid region, and one cervical lymph node enlargement which was oval, mobile and tender on palpation. The intra oral exam (Figure 2) showed an adequate oral hygiene. There was no evidence of caries or other dental anomalies. The mucosa was moist and well lubricated. An erythema around the Stensen´s duct opening was noted and a serious but not purulent discharge was seen on pressing the parotid glands. The diagnosis of viral parotitis was proposed.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (a, b, c). a: Sialendoscopic view of pale parotid duct mucosa in a patient with juvenile recurrent parotitis; caption explicitly describes endoscopic appearance of pale mucosa. b: Endoscopic view of a parotid duct stenosis being overpassed with a guidewire in JRP; ductal stenosis matches the vocabulary finding ductal_stricture. c: Endoscopic view of mucus within the main salivary duct in a JRP patient; caption explicitly states mucus in the main salivary duct.
panels.attribution_text: Pušnik et al. Sialendoscopy in Management of Juvenile Recurrent Parotitis-A Single Centre Experience.. Children (Basel, Switzerland) 2022. doi:10.3390/children9111632. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 2.
panels.figure_caption: Sialendoscopic appearance of the parotid duct. (a) displays the endoscopic appearance of pale mucosa. (b) depicts guiding wire introduced during the sialendoscopic procedure to overpass the stenosis. (c) shows mucus in the main salivary duct.
in_text_mentions: During the procedure, the main duct was examined—there was a pale appearance of ductal wall, individual capillaries, and mucous plugs noted to various extent within all patients (Figure 2). Eight patients (38%) had stenosis present and seven had stenosis with a grade of S2 or higher. The mean depth of endoscope introduction into the duct system was 59.1 ± 13.6 mm (range, 22–87 mm). During two procedures, the ductal wall was damaged, therefore we stopped the intervention. In both, steroids were instilled into the duct before this event, and later restitutio ad integrum state was re-established.
